messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 28
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Social Media Manager
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Driving with Others: Driving with people, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Uniform or Weapons: Military, police uniforms or weapons, Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Military Trauma and the Distance Between Worlds

Marcus was twenty-two when the IED detonated thirty meters from his Humvee during a patrol outside Kandahar. He remembers the sound—a percussion that seemed to come from everywhere at once—and then a strange, suspended moment where his body registered the blast but his mind had not yet caught up. When awareness returned, it came in fragments: the smell of burnt metal and something else he could not name, the weight of his own limbs feeling disconnected, and the sight of Corporal Diaz's left leg, the one that had been beside him seconds before, now a separate thing on the ground. The medics got there quickly. Marcus had trained for this. But training and reality had turned out to be entirely different things.

Now, six years later at twenty-eight, Marcus worked as a social media manager for a mid-sized marketing firm in Denver, a job that was supposed to feel far removed from all of that. He was good at it—strategic, detail-oriented, quick with language. But the distance between the office and Kandahar had compressed into something much smaller than geography.

The triggers came without warning, though Marcus had learned to anticipate them with a kind of constant low-level dread. A video on his feed of a construction accident with visible lacerations would send his nervous system into overdrive; his hands would shake, and he would feel his chest tighten as though the blast were happening again, right there in his cubicle. He had started scrolling with his eyes half-closed, trying to catch and avoid graphic content before it fully registered. His colleagues had noticed him flinching at their screens but said nothing. When his girlfriend, Sophia, suggested they drive up to Boulder for a weekend, something in him seized. The thought of sitting in the passenger seat while she drove, trapped in the metal box with no control, his body unable to move or escape—he had declined, invented a work deadline. She had not pushed, but he had seen the disappointment settle into her face.

The helicopter sounds were the worst. Denver's medical helicopter made regular runs, and when Marcus heard that distant whump-whump-whump, his entire body would lock. His heart would race as though he were still twenty-two, as though the next sound would be the one that changed everything. He had taken to wearing earbuds during his lunch breaks, even sitting alone in the office break room, just to have some control over what he heard.

Sleep had become a negotiation with his own mind. Marcus would lie awake for hours, his body wound tight, convinced that if he allowed himself to drift off, something catastrophic would happen. The need to stay alert—to maintain that vigilant watch—felt as essential as breathing. When sleep finally came, it was shallow and fractured, interrupted by dreams he could not quite remember but that left him gasping and drenched in sweat. Sophia had started sleeping in the guest room. She had not said it was because of his thrashing or his sudden, violent startle when she reached over to touch him in the dark, but they both knew.

What troubled Marcus most was the way the memory of that day had become almost unreal to him, even as its emotional weight never diminished. He could recall individual moments—the taste of dust, the feeling of his own blood on his neck—but they did not connect into a coherent story. It was as though his mind had shattered the event into pieces that refused to fit together, and when he tried to make sense of it, the whole thing felt impossible, too extreme to have actually happened. Yet the feeling remained: a constant, suffocating sense that something terrible was about to occur.

Over the months, Marcus had begun to believe that he was fundamentally broken in a way that could not be repaired. He had started avoiding anything that stressed his body—he no longer went to the gym, no longer played the recreational soccer he had once loved. He rehearsed conversations before meetings, scripting every exchange, trying to control outcomes because the world felt too unpredictable, too dangerous. He could not watch police procedurals or military films; the sight of a uniform, even on a television screen, would send him spiraling. Most painfully, he had come to see himself as permanently different from the people around him, as though the blast had drawn a line between who he had been and who he could never be again. Sophia loved him, he knew that, but he was certain that someone else—someone who had not been broken in Kandahar—would have been a better partner, would not have brought this weight into her life.

It was Sophia, finally, who insisted he seek help. She had found a therapist who specialized in trauma, and though Marcus felt the old resistance rising—the conviction that talking would not undo what had been done—he had made the appointment. He was afraid that if he began to unpack this, he would discover that the damage was even worse than he believed. But he was also, quietly, hoping that someone could help him understand why a moment six years in the past still held him captive in the present.
